newsitem.title: USA: IMF paints bleak picture of European economy.
newsitem.headline: IMF paints bleak picture of European economy.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday painted a bleak picture of Europe as a region plagued by sky-high unemployment and boxed in by its drive to launch a single currency in 1999.

While European Union nations are generally expected to enjoy faster economic growth in 1997, many remain saddled with deep-seated problems that will require tough action to solve, the IMF said in its semi-annual World Economic Outlook.
Those problems include labour markets that do not seem to work well and government budget deficits that remain too high and hinder long-term growth.
"The real risk in Europe is that ... unemployment rates could continue their steady upward march," the IMF said. "This underscores the urgency of tackling the problem more forcefully."
In the short-run, the Fund sees better times ahead for Europe. Growth throughout the European Union is expected to average 2.5 percent next year, up from 1.6 percent in 1996.
Unemployment is projected to slip to an average of 11 percent in 1997, from 11.4 percent this year.

The IMF though warned that its economic projections could prove too optimistic, especially if Europe's headlong drive to cut budget deficits under the Maastricht Treaty acts as more of a drag on growth than expected.
The Maastricht treaty sets out tough budget guidelines that European Union countries must meet in 1997 for entry into European Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.

"The recovery in Europe may be weaker than projected because it may be restrained ... by the short-term contractionary effects of fiscal consolidation efforts being implemented in most EU countries partly to satisfy the Maastricht criteria by 1997," the IMF said.
Paradoxically, if growth is held back by the drive to slash budget deficits, that will make satisfying the Maastricht criteria that much more difficult.
Slower growth tends to bloat budget deficits by pushing up government spending on uenmployment and other benefits and depressing tax revenues from economic activity.

The IMF said it expected Germany and France -- perhaps the two countries most important to a successful launch of EMU -- to satisfy the Maastricht criteria. But it made clear that depended on economic growth picking up as expected.

If growth does not strengthen, the IMF signalled it would prefer European nations to temporarily allow their budget deficits to rise in line with the weakness of their economies rather than to cut them to meet the tough Maastricht criteria.
"It is important to avoid aggravating a difficult situation through unduly procyclical (tight) fiscal policies," the Fund said.

Whatever the short-term problems posed by Maastricht, the IMf made clear that in the medium term European countries need to put their public finances in order. But that will require reining in spending in such politically explosive areas as pensions and unemployment benefits.
It linked Europe's high budget deficits to its excessive unemployment. Europe's high unemployment bloats deficits by pushing up spending and robbing governments of tax revenues.
The IMF said comprehensive labour market reforms would be needed to really drive down unemployment. Faster economic growth would help, but there was a limit on how much it could do.

"As much as eight to nine percentage points of the EU's current unemployment rate of over 11 percent is widely considered to be structural in the sense that it is unlikely that it could be absorbed through cyclical recovery alone, without significant inflationary risks," the Fund said.
It accused European governments of "excessive timidity" in tackling the problem and recommended a whole set of reforms.

They included: reduced unemployment benefits with tighter eligibility criteria and of shorter duration; lower payroll taxes, particularly for low-wage workers; minimum wage cuts; and changes in the way governments handle collective bargaining agreements.
